keyVerseText: But when Paul had appealed to be reserved unto the hearing of Augustus, I commanded him to be kept till I might send him to Caesar. hearing: or, judgment
rootMeaning: The Greek adjective σεβαστός (sebastós) derives from the verb σεβάζομαι (sebázomai), which means 'to worship' or 'to venerate.' This root conveys a sense of reverence and adoration, suggesting that σεβαστός originally carried the idea of being worthy of profound respect or honor. Beyond the English gloss of 'Augustus' or 'imperial,' the root sense emphasizes a status that inspires awe and devotion, reflecting both religious and political veneration.
usageInScripture: In Scripture, σεβαστός appears three times and is consistently connected to the Roman Emperor Augustus, either as a title or an adjective describing imperial authority. The top translations show it rendered as 'of Augustus' twice and 'Augustus' once, indicating its primary use as a formal, honorific designation rather than a general adjective. This limited but focused usage highlights the word's specialized function in the New Testament context, especially in relation to Roman governance and authority.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding σεβαστός as rooted in worship and reverence enriches our grasp of the cultural and political backdrop of the New Testament. The term's association with the emperor, who was often venerated in a quasi-divine manner, contrasts with the Christian call to worship God alone. This tension underscores the uniqueness of Christ's lordship over all earthly powers and reminds believers that true reverence belongs to God rather than any human ruler. The word thus invites reflection on the proper object of worship and the supremacy of Christ as King and Lord.
keyVerseReflection: Acts 25:21 states, 'But when Paul had appealed to be reserved unto the hearing of Augustus, I commanded him to be kept till I might send him to Caesar.' Here, σεβαστός identifies the Roman Emperor Augustus, highlighting the political authority before whom Paul’s case would be heard. The use of σεβαστός conveys not just a title but the weight of imperial power and honor, setting the stage for the gospel to confront worldly authority. It reminds us that the gospel transcends human institutions, even those as august as the emperor himself.
